claim: A total of 756 replicate P. aeruginosa populations were challenged with sequential treatments across three fully independent evolution experiments.
source: We challenged a total of 756 replicate P. aeruginosa populations with sequential treatments across three fully independent evolution experiments, each focused on a different set of three antibiotics (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1A, Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of populations and experiments conducted.

claim: Antibiotic concentrations were calibrated to an inhibitory concentration of 75% (IC75).
source: The antibiotic concentrations were calibrated to an inhibitory concentration of 75% (IC75), allowing bacteria to adapt to the imposed selection pressure.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the calibration method used.

claim: Populations were propagated with a transfer to fresh medium every 12 hr (one transfer) across a total of 96 transfers, equivalent to approximately 500 bacterial generations.
source: We used a serial dilution protocol for experimental evolution, with 2% culture transfer after 12 hr (one transfer) across a total of 96 transfers, equivalent to approximately 500 bacterial generations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental protocol and duration.

claim: The two β-lactam sets produced a high degree of extinction (CAR-CEF-DOR: 27.2% and TIC-AZL-CEZ: 13.3%).
source: The two β-lactam sets produced a surprisingly high degree of extinction (CAR-CEF-DOR and TIC-AZL-CEZ; extinct fraction 27.2 and 13.3%, respectively, Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific extinction percentages and references Figure 1C showing the data.

claim: The observed extinction frequency for β-lactam sets was comparable to that observed in the previous experiment with CAR-CIP-GEN (extinct fraction 15%).
source: The observed extinction frequency was comparable to that observed in the previous experiment with CAR-CIP-GEN (extinct fraction 15%, Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript compares current results with previous experimental data.

claim: CIP-DOR-STR caused no extinction.
source: CIP-DOR-STR caused no extinction, indicating that extinction was not explained by applying heterogeneous sets of antibiotics.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the extinction outcome for this antibiotic combination.

claim: Treatments that switched between antibiotics fast (every transfer) produced much higher extinction levels than those that switched slowly (every four transfers) or not at all.
source: Within the β-lactam sequential treatments, we observed that treatments that switched between antibiotics fast (every transfer) produced much higher extinction levels than those that switched slowly (every four transfers) or not at all (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between switching rate and extinction with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Most of the extinction events happened early in the experiment.
source: Most of the extinction events happened early in the experiment (Figure 1E), indicating that the initial treatment steps are critical for adaptation of populations.
evidence: The manuscript states the timing of extinction events with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Fast sequential β-lactam treatments showed a surprising ability to restrict bacterial adaptation.
source: We conclude that fast sequential β-lactam treatments showed a surprising ability to restrict bacterial adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on extinction and adaptation.

claim: The early phase dynamics were characterized by significantly decelerated adaptation dynamics of the fast-regular group compared with monotherapy and slow-regular.
source: The early phase dynamics were characterized by significantly decelerated adaptation dynamics of the fast-regular group compared with monotherapy and slow-regular (GLM, post hoc test, p<0.037, Supplementary file 1B), but not random treatments.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis results comparing adaptation dynamics.

claim: The slow-regular treatment did not differ significantly from monotherapy or random treatments.
source: The slow-regular treatment did not differ significantly from monotherapy or random treatments (GLM, post hoc test, p=0.469, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison results.

claim: Growth yields of the groups converged to a plateau of roughly 90% relative yield in the subsequent phase.
source: In the subsequent phase, growth yields of the groups converged to a plateau of roughly 90% relative yield, indicating similar final levels of adaptation (the growth yields of main treatment groups showed no statistical differences in phases 2 and 3, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the convergence of growth yields with statistical support.

claim: In fast sequential treatments, bacterial growth in the transfers with DOR was lower than in the transfers with the other two antibiotics.
source: Intriguingly, in these fast sequential treatments, bacterial growth in the transfers with DOR was lower than in the transfers with the other two antibiotics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating an evolutionary constraint associated with the antibiotic DOR.
evidence: The manuscript describes differential growth patterns with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: All treatments were initiated using specifically standardized IC75 dosage.
source: All treatments were initiated using specifically standardized IC75 dosage (see Materials and methods) and at the IC75, DOR showed very little variation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the standardization of antibiotic dosage.

claim: The observed evolutionary constraint may be due to lower rate of DOR resistance emergence.
source: We thus hypothesize that the observed evolutionary constraint may be due to lower rate of DOR resistance emergence.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on the observed data.

claim: Resistance to the used β-lactams increased across the two time points only in some treatments, but not all.
source: Resistance to the used β-lactams increased across the two time points only in some treatments, but not all (Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 1F), suggesting treatment-dependent evolutionary responses to the antibiotics.
evidence: The manuscript describes variable resistance evolution with reference to multiple figures.

claim: Most treatment types varied significantly from each other in their multidrug β-lactam resistance in both phases.
source: Most treatment types varied significantly from each other in their multidrug β-lactam resistance in both phases (Supplementary file 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of resistance differences.

claim: The multidrug resistance in the early phase was in most cases constrained by the susceptibility to DOR.
source: The multidrug resistance in the early phase was in most cases constrained by the susceptibility to DOR (e.g., in the switching and monotherapy treatments).
evidence: The manuscript identifies DOR susceptibility as a constraining factor.

claim: Population diversity was significantly higher at transfer 48 as compared to transfer 12.
source: We found population diversity to be significantly higher at transfer 48 as compared to transfer 12 (ANOVA, F = 6.2060, p=0.01893, Supplementary file 1E), indicating a diversification of the evolving lineages over time.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of population diversity over time.

claim: All isolates, except those that received DOR monotherapy, had mutations in known resistance genes by the end of the early phase.
source: We found that all isolates, except those that received DOR monotherapy, had mutations in known resistance genes by the end of the early phase (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports genomic sequencing results with reference to Table 1.

claim: Isolates from the DOR monotherapy did not show a noticeable amount of resistance at the early phase.
source: This agreed with the inferred resistance profiles where isolates from the DOR monotherapy did not show a noticeable amount of resistance at that stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes resistance phenotypes with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: DOR resistance was found at the end of the middle phase, mirrored by a non-synonymous mutation in the gene ftsI.
source: DOR resistance was, however, found at the end of the middle phase (Figure 2C), and this was mirrored in the genomics with a non-synonymous mutation in the gene ftsI.
evidence: The manuscript correlates phenotypic resistance with genetic changes.

claim: The gene ftsI codes for the penicillin binding protein 3 (PBP3), a common target of the three β-lactams.
source: This gene codes for the penicillin binding protein 3 (PBP3) (Liao and Hancock, 1995), a common target of the three β-lactams (Davies et al., 2008; Fontana et al., 2000; Rodriguez‐Tebár et al., 1982; Rodríguez-Tebar et al., 1982; Zimmermann, 1980).
evidence: The manuscript provides information about gene function with citations.

claim: Isolates from CAR monotherapy contained ftsI mutations at a different site within the gene and associated with a different resistance profile than the DOR-associated ftsI variant.
source: ftsI was also found to be mutated in isolates from CAR monotherapy, although at a different site within the gene and associated with a different resistance profile than the DOR-associated ftsI variant (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes mutation specificity with reference to resistance profiles.

claim: Isolates from CEF monotherapy contained mutations in pepA.
source: Isolates from CEF monotherapy contained mutations in pepA.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific mutations found in genomic analysis.

claim: pepA is responsible for the production of a protein required for cytotoxicity and virulence in P. aeruginosa.
source: This gene is responsible for the production of a protein required for cytotoxicity and virulence in P. aeruginosa (Hauser et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript provides gene function information with citation.

claim: pepA was previously found to be mutated in P. aeruginosa strains resistant to certain β-lactams.
source: Although its role in antimicrobial resistance remains to be studied in detail, it was previously found to be mutated in P. aeruginosa strains resistant to certain β-lactams (Cabot et al., 2018; Sanz-García et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies linking pepA to resistance.

claim: The switching treatments selected for mutations in nalD and phoQ.
source: In particular, we identified mutations in nalD and phoQ, a negative regulator of the MexAB-OprM efflux pump and a two-component system, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific mutations found in switching treatments.

claim: Mutations in nalD and phoQ account for resistance to a variety of drugs in P. aeruginosa.
source: Mutations in these genes account for resistance to a variety of drugs in P. aeruginosa (Barbosa et al., 2021; Sobel et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the role of these genes in resistance.

claim: Mutations were identified in some non-canonical β-lactam resistance genes such as rmcA, 23srRNA, 3-oxoacyl synthase, dnaX, and zipA.
source: Further mutations were identified in some non-canonical β-lactam resistance genes such as rmcA, 23srRNA, 3-oxoacyl synthase, dnaX, and zipA (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports additional mutations found in genomic analysis.

claim: DOR resistance mutations were found only later in the experiment, consistent with the obtained resistance profiles.
source: Taken together, mutations in both canonical and non-canonical targets of β-lactam selection were identified in our experiment, and among these, DOR resistance mutations were found only later in the experiment, consistent with the obtained resistance profiles (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the timing of DOR resistance evolution.

claim: Negative hysteresis existed for several switches between the β-lactams.
source: We found that negative hysteresis existed for several switches between the β-lactams (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports hysteresis measurements with reference to figures.

claim: DOR and CAR displayed asymmetric bidirectional negative hysteresis with the switch from DOR to CAR resulting in stronger negative hysteresis than the reverse.
source: DOR and CAR displayed asymmetric bidirectional negative hysteresis with the switch from DOR to CAR, resulting in stronger negative hysteresis than the reverse.
evidence: The manuscript describes specific hysteresis patterns between antibiotics.

claim: Negative hysteresis was also observed in the switch from CAR to CEF and CEF to CEF.
source: Negative hysteresis was also observed in the switch from CAR to CEF and CEF to CEF.
evidence: The manuscript reports additional hysteresis observations.

claim: Only a single case of weak positive hysteresis was observed.
source: To our surprise, only a single case of weak positive hysteresis was observed, although we generally anticipated it given that P. aeruginosa produces the AmpC β-lactamase (Livermore, 1995).
evidence: The manuscript reports an unexpected finding with reference to known bacterial characteristics.

claim: The spontaneous resistance rate was significantly lower for DOR than for CAR and CEF.
source: We found that the spontaneous resistance rate was significantly lower for DOR than for CAR and CEF (likelihood ratio test, p<0.0001 and p<0.01, respectively; Supplementary file 1H, Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of spontaneous resistance rates.

claim: Cross-resistance effects were particularly common towards CAR (93% of clones with spontaneous CEF resistance and 71% with DOR resistance).
source: Moreover, the resulting cross-resistance effects (Figure 4C) were particularly common towards CAR (93% of clones with spontaneous CEF resistance and 71% with DOR resistance)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of cross-resistance with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Cross-resistance to CEF was observed in 73% of originally CAR-resistant clones and 67% of DOR-resistant clones.
source: and CEF (73% of originally CAR-resistant clones and 67% DOR-resistant clones).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of cross-resistance.

claim: The smallest levels of cross-resistance were expressed towards DOR (36% of originally CAR-resistant clones and 50% CEF-resistant clones).
source: By contrast, the smallest levels of cross-resistance were expressed towards DOR (36% of originally CAR-resistant clones and 50% CEF-resistant clones).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of cross-resistance.

claim: The overall fraction of cross-resistant clones was significantly smaller towards DOR than either CEF or CAR.
source: The overall fraction of cross-resistant clones was significantly smaller towards DOR than either CEF or CAR (Fisher's exact test, p<0.0004; Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis of cross-resistance patterns.

claim: Of the three β-lactams, DOR had the lowest probability for both direct and indirect resistance.
source: We conclude that of the three β-lactams DOR had the lowest probability for both direct and indirect resistance, thereby providing experimental support to the indication of constrained DOR resistance evolution obtained from the detailed phenotypic and genomic characterization of the evolved bacteria (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Extinction was significantly associated with switching rate.
source: Our analysis revealed that extinction was significantly associated with both the experimental predictors, switching rate (GLM, F = 14.44, p=0.0042, Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1J–M)
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis results.

claim: Extinction was significantly associated with temporal irregularity.
source: and temporal irregularity (GLM, F = 10.53, p=0.0101, Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis results.

claim: Temporal irregularity showed a statistical trend with multidrug resistance.
source: Temporal irregularity further showed a statistical trend with multidrug resistance (GLM, F = 4.19, p=0.0711, Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical trend.

claim: The cumulative cross-resistant fraction showed a significant association with extinction.
source: From our biological predictors, the cumulative cross-resistant fraction showed a significant association with extinction (GLM, F = 10.42, p=0.0121, Supplementary file 1O)
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis results.

claim: Cumulative probability of spontaneous resistance showed a statistical trend with extinction.
source: while cumulative probability of spontaneous resistance showed a statistical trend (GLM, F = 4.14, p=0.0763, Supplementary file 1O).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical trend.

claim: The cumulative cross-resistant fraction is strongly correlated with extinction.
source: Indeed, the cumulative cross-resistant fraction and also the cumulative probability of spontaneous resistance are strongly correlated with extinction (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript describes correlation with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The cumulative cross-resistant fraction is strongly correlated with switching rate.
source: The cumulative cross-resistant fraction is also strongly correlated with switching rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), most likely explaining the latter impact on extinction.
evidence: The manuscript describes correlation with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Cumulative hysteresis levels did not have a significant influence on any of the evolutionary responses.
source: By contrast, cumulative hysteresis levels did not have a significant influence on any of the evolutionary responses (GLM, F = 0.16, p=0.7015, Supplementary file 1O).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis results.

claim: In sequential CAR-CEF-DOR treatments, the switching rate, temporal irregularity of antibiotics, the probability of spontaneous resistance, and especially the resulting collateral effects determine treatment efficacy through their effect on bacterial extinction.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that in our sequential CAR-CEF-DOR treatments the switching rate, temporal irregularity of antibiotics, the probability of spontaneous resistance, and especially the resulting collateral effects (maximized by switching rate) determine treatment efficacy through their effect on bacterial extinction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple statistical analyses.

claim: The limiting factor appears to be constrained evolution of resistance and low levels of cross-resistance to DOR.
source: The limiting factor appears to be constrained evolution of resistance and low levels of cross-resistance to DOR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with multiple β-lactam antibiotics is generally avoided due to the perceived fear of therapy failure from cross-resistance.
source: Treatment with multiple β-lactam antibiotics is generally avoided due to the perceived fear of therapy failure from cross-resistance.
evidence: This is stated as a general practice in the field.

claim: Sets of three β-lactams constrained bacterial adaptation by reducing bacterial survival.
source: We characterized the ability of replicate P. aeruginosa populations to evolve de novo resistance to sequential treatments with different drug sets. To our surprise, we found that sets of three β-lactams constrained bacterial adaptation by reducing bacterial survival.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: Treatment potency was determined by variation in the spontaneous rate of resistance to the β-lactams and the resulting collateral effects across sequential treatment protocols.
source: We demonstrate that treatment potency was determined by variation in the spontaneous rate of resistance to the β-lactams and the resulting collateral effects across sequential treatment protocols.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The triple β-lactam sequences are at least as effective at causing extinction as sequences of antibiotics with distinct modes of actions.
source: Our initial screen of sequential protocols with different antibiotic triplets revealed that the triple β-lactam sequences are at least as effective at causing extinction as sequences of antibiotics with distinct modes of actions.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative experimental results.

claim: The β-lactam aztreonam was shown to interact synergistically with four other β-lactam drugs against multiple resistant isolates of Enterobacteriaceae and P. aeruginosa in vitro.
source: For example, the β-lactam aztreonam was shown to interact synergistically with four other β-lactam drugs against multiple resistant isolates of Enterobacteriaceae and P. aeruginosa in vitro (Buesing and Jorgensen, 1984).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on β-lactam combinations.

claim: A combination of ticarcillin with ceftazidime produced high efficacy in a rat peritonitis model.
source: A combination of ticarcillin with ceftazidime produced high efficacy in a rat peritonitis model (Shyu et al., 1987).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on β-lactam combinations.

claim: In a treatment of bacterial soft tissue infections, the combination of cefotaxime and mecillinam led to higher clinical response rates than the tested monotherapy.
source: In a treatment of bacterial soft tissue infections, the combination of cefotaxime and mecillinam led to higher clinical response rates than the tested monotherapy (File and Tan, 1983).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous clinical research on β-lactam combinations.

claim: The dual β-lactam combination of ceftazidime plus piperacillin was as effective as the combination of ceftazidime and tobramycin in granulocytopenic cancer patients.
source: Further, the dual β-lactam combination of ceftazidime plus piperacillin was as effective as the combination of ceftazidime and tobramycin in granulocytopenic cancer patients (Joshi et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous clinical research on β-lactam combinations.

claim: A triple combination of meropenem, piperacillin, and tazobactam successfully constrained resistance evolution in MRSA, both in vitro and in a mouse model.
source: More recent studies demonstrated that a triple combination of meropenem, piperacillin, and tazobactam successfully constrained resistance evolution in Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), both in vitro and in a mouse model (Gonzales et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent research on β-lactam combinations.

claim: The combination of cefotaxime and mecillinam was effective against Salmonella enterica harboring a mutant β-lactamase in a mouse model.
source: In addition, the combination of cefotaxime and mecillinam was effective against Salmonella enterica harboring a mutant β-lactamase in a mouse model (Rosenkilde et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent research on β-lactam combinations.

claim: The use of multiple β-lactams, either as a combination or sequentially, is a commonly underappreciated form of therapy.
source: We conclude that the use of multiple β-lactams, either as a combination or sequentially, is a commonly underappreciated form of therapy and its use opens new avenues to better utilize our existing antibiotic armamentarium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings and literature review.

claim: Spontaneous rate of antibiotic resistance played a critical role in the success of the CAR-CEF-DOR sequential treatment.
source: Spontaneous rate of antibiotic resistance was found to play a critical role in the success of the CAR-CEF-DOR sequential treatment.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The probability of spontaneous resistance on all three β-lactams was significantly different, with the rate of DOR resistance being the lowest.
source: The probability of spontaneous resistance on all three β-lactams was significantly different, with the rate of DOR resistance being the lowest.
evidence: This summarizes the fluctuation assay results.

claim: These rates determined the overall probability of acquiring direct resistance in treatment, which significantly correlated with the frequency of population extinction.
source: These rates determined the overall probability of acquiring direct resistance in treatment, which significantly correlated with the frequency of population extinction (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the relationship between resistance rates and extinction.

claim: Resistance rates were previously shown to vary towards different antibiotics in E. coli and P. aeruginosa.
source: Resistance rates were previously shown to vary towards different antibiotics, for example, in Escherichia coli (El Meouche and Dunlop, 2018) and P. aeruginosa (Oliver et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on resistance rate variation.

claim: Variation in resistance rates can arise from genetic factors such as mutational target space and physiological factors like activation of the bacterial SOS response.
source: This variation can arise from genetic factors such as mutational target space and physiological factors like activation of the bacterial SOS response (Martinez and Baquero, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on mechanisms of resistance rate variation.

claim: Antibiotics that target multiple pathways in a cell are considered advantageous for reducing resistance emergence.
source: Such information on resistance rates has so far been used for predicting the occurrence of resistance against single drugs, and antibiotics that target multiple pathways in a cell are considered advantageous in this context (Ross-Gillespie and Kümmerli, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on antibiotic design principles.

claim: Compounds against S. aureus that inhibit both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV are examples of antibiotics targeting multiple pathways.
source: One example of the latter are compounds against S. aureus that inhibit both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV (Nyerges et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites an example from previous research.

claim: The rate of resistance emergence may be reduced by using adjuvants that target the SOS response.
source: The rate of resistance emergence may also be reduced by using adjuvants that target the SOS response (Bell and MacLean, 2018), as previously shown for compounds interfering with LexA activity leading to reduced resistance rates to ciprofloxacin and rifampicin in E. coli (Cirz et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on adjuvant strategies.

claim: Inclusion of an antibiotic with relatively low spontaneous resistance emergence can enhance the potency of a sequential treatment design.
source: Our study extends the role of resistance rates of antibiotics beyond this convention. We show that inclusion of an antibiotic with relatively low spontaneous resistance emergence can enhance the potency of a sequential treatment design.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: DOR belongs to the carbapenem subclass of the β-lactam antibiotics.
source: DOR belongs to the carbapenem subclass of the β-lactam antibiotics.
evidence: This is a statement of antibiotic classification.

claim: Carbapenems possess broad activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Carbapenems possess broad activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Papp-Wallace et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on carbapenem properties.

claim: Carbapenems are active against many β-lactamase-producing microbes since their thiazolidinic ring makes them relatively resistant to β-lactamase-mediated hydrolysis.
source: and are active against many β-lactamase-producing microbes since their thiazolidinic ring makes them relatively resistant to β-lactamase-mediated hydrolysis (Schafer et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on carbapenem mechanism.

claim: The penicillin CAR is active mostly (albeit not exclusively) against Gram-negative bacteria.
source: In contrast, the penicillin CAR is active mostly (albeit not exclusively) against Gram-negative bacteria (Castle, 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on CAR activity spectrum.

claim: The activity of the cephalosporin CEF is restricted to P. aeruginosa.
source: while the activity of the cephalosporin CEF is restricted to P. aeruginosa (Wright, 1986).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on CEF activity spectrum.

claim: All three antibiotics (CAR, CEF, DOR) show high potency against a large variety of clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa.
source: Within P. aeruginosa, all three antibiotics show high potency against a large variety of clinical isolates (Castanheira et al., 2009; Neu and Scully, 1984; Traub and Raymond, 1970).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on antibiotic potency.

claim: DOR has a particularly low propensity to select for resistance mutations, even when compared to other carbapenems.
source: Resistance rates for β-lactam antibiotics were assessed with different approaches across P. aeruginosa strains and clinical isolates, consistently showing that DOR has a particularly low propensity to select for resistance mutations, even when compared to other carbapenems (Barbosa et al., 2017; Barbosa et al., 2021; Sakyo et al., 2006; Tanimoto et al., 2008; Mushtaq et al., 2004; Fujimura et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple previous studies on DOR resistance rates.

claim: The phenotype of reduced spontaneous resistance to DOR appears to be robustly expressed across different P. aeruginosa genotypes and does not extend to other carbapenems or β-lactams.
source: Therefore, the phenotype of reduced spontaneous resistance to DOR appears to be robustly expressed across different P. aeruginosa genotypes and does not extend to other carbapenems or β-lactams.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cited literature.

claim: One possible reason for DOR's low resistance rate may be variation in the range of β-lactam target proteins, where DOR binds more PBPs than do CAR or CEF.
source: One possible reason for this pattern may be variation in the range of β-lactam target proteins, in this case the penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), and where DOR is known to bind more of these PBPs than do CAR or CEF (Davies et al., 2008; Fontana et al., 2000; Rodriguez‐Tebár et al., 1982; Rodríguez-Tebar et al., 1982; Zapun et al., 2008; Zimmermann, 1980).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on PBP binding and proposes a mechanism.

claim: Target resistance to DOR would likely require a larger number of mutations than that to other β-lactams.
source: One possible reason for this pattern may be variation in the range of β-lactam target proteins, in this case the penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), and where DOR is known to bind more of these PBPs than do CAR or CEF (Davies et al., 2008; Fontana et al., 2000; Rodriguez‐Tebár et al., 1982; Rodríguez-Tebar et al., 1982; Zapun et al., 2008; Zimmermann, 1980). Thus, target resistance to DOR would likely require a larger number of mutations than that to other β-lactams.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the multiple target binding property.

claim: Another carbapenem, meropenem, targets the same PBPs as DOR but has a higher resistance rate.
source: Interestingly, another carbapenem, meropenem, targets the same PBPs as DOR (Davies et al., 2008) but has a higher resistance rate, suggesting that the underlying reasons for resistance rate variation are multifactorial.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research and draws an inference about complexity.

claim: Effective resistance mutations against DOR seem to be less commonly available in P. aeruginosa in comparison to that against other drugs, including CEF and CAR.
source: Taken together, effective resistance mutations against DOR seem to be less commonly available in P. aeruginosa in comparison to that against other drugs, including the here used CEF and CAR.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the discussion of DOR properties.

claim: A key determinant of treatment potency was the reduced level of spontaneous cross-resistance to the sequentially applied drugs.
source: A key determinant of treatment potency was the reduced level of spontaneous cross-resistance to the sequentially applied drugs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The findings are consistent with the previously and repeatedly proposed importance of collateral sensitivity for the efficacy of sequential treatment protocols.
source: Our findings are consistent with the previously and repeatedly proposed importance of collateral sensitivity for the efficacy of sequential treatment protocols (Barbosa et al., 2019; Hernando-Amado et al., 2020; Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Kim et al., 2014; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Yen and Papin, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript relates findings to previous research.

claim: The lack of cross-resistance indicates that mutant cells which have become resistant to one drug maintain at least ancestral levels of susceptibility against the second drug.
source: Even though we did not measure collateral sensitivity directly, the lack of cross-resistance is related as it indicates that the mutant cells, which have become resistant to one drug, maintain at least ancestral levels of susceptibility against the second drug.
evidence: This explains the relationship between lack of cross-resistance and collateral sensitivity.

claim: The study focused on spontaneous emergence of cross-resistance (or lack thereof).
source: Moreover, our study focused on spontaneous emergence of cross-resistance (or lack thereof).
evidence: This describes the specific approach of the study.

claim: Many previous studies established collateral effects after bacteria evolved resistance to the first drug over many generations, often followed by only a single antibiotic switch.
source: By contrast, many previous studies established collateral effects after bacteria evolved resistance to the first drug over many generations, often followed by only a single antibiotic switch to assess the impact of collateral sensitivity on therapy success (Barbosa et al., 2019; Hernando-Amado et al., 2020; Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Yen and Papin, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript contrasts the current approach with previous studies.

claim: The study revealed potentially beneficial collateral effects between antibiotics of the same class.
source: Surprisingly, our study revealed potentially beneficial collateral effects between antibiotics of the same class.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: The three β-lactams were chosen because previous work demonstrated cross-resistance between most of them, although inferred upon multigenerational adaptation to the first drug.
source: In fact, we chose these three β-lactams because our previous work demonstrated cross-resistance between most of them, although inferred upon multigenerational adaptation to the first drug (Barbosa et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for antibiotic selection.

claim: The finding of a lack of cross-resistance among some of these drugs suggests that spontaneous mutants may have different collateral profiles than the lines which adapted over many generations.
source: Our current finding of a lack of cross-resistance among some of these drugs now suggests that spontaneous mutants may have different collateral profiles than the lines, which adapted over many generations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing current and previous results.

claim: The collateral effects of spontaneous mutants are likely to be more pertinent for the design of sequential treatments with fast switches among antibiotics.
source: Our results further suggest that the collateral effects of spontaneous mutants are likely to be more pertinent for the design of sequential treatments with fast switches among antibiotics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The efficacy of fast sequential treatments was optimized by considering collateral effects for single-step mutants of S. aureus obtained after 20 hr exposure to three distinct antibiotics.
source: This suggestion is supported by two previous studies, in which the efficacy of fast sequential treatments was optimized by considering collateral effects for either single-step mutants of S. aureus, obtained after 20 hr exposure to three distinct antibiotics for 20 hr (Kim et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research supporting the conclusion.

claim: The efficacy of fast sequential treatments was optimized by considering collateral effects from E. faecalis populations adapted over 2 days to four distinct antibiotics.
source: or from Enterococcus faecalis populations adapted over 2 days to four distinct antibiotics (Maltas and Wood, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research supporting the conclusion.

claim: Almost all treatments caused the evolution of collateral sensitivity towards the aminoglycoside gentamicin, but not the fluoroquinolone ciprofloxacin.
source: As a side note, it is particularly interesting that our detailed resistance analysis consistently revealed almost all treatments to cause the evolution of collateral sensitivity towards the aminoglycoside gentamicin, but not the fluoroquinolone ciprofloxacin (Figure 2B, C), possibly indicating yet another treatment option – in cases where the applied triple β-lactam sequential protocols fail.
evidence: The manuscript reports an additional finding with reference to figures.

claim: Temporal irregularity was found to constrain bacterial adaptation.
source: Temporal irregularity was additionally found to constrain bacterial adaptation.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claim: When bacteria experienced the antibiotics in an irregular pattern, this caused significantly increased extinction and to some degree reduced multidrug resistance.
source: When bacteria experienced the antibiotics in an irregular pattern, this caused significantly increased extinction and to some degree reduced multidrug resistance.
evidence: The manuscript describes the effects of temporal irregularity.

claim: With CAR-DOR-CEF, the lowest multidrug resistance was observed in random sequential treatments.
source: With CAR-DOR-CEF, the lowest multidrug resistance was observed in random sequential treatments (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), as also previously observed with CIP-GEN-CAR (Roemhild et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific finding with reference to a figure and previous study.

claim: Environmental change anticipation has been documented in several microorganisms.
source: Environmental change anticipation has been documented in several microorganisms (Mitchell et al., 2009; Mitchell and Pilpel, 2011), indicating their capability to specifically adapt to regular environmental change.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on microbial adaptation.

claim: Stochastic changes can make it harder to evolve anticipation.
source: Stochastic changes can make it harder to evolve anticipation (Roemhild and Schulenburg, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on evolutionary constraints.

claim: Stochastic changes in environmental parameters were found to constrain fitness in evolving bacteria and viruses.
source: Stochastic changes in environmental parameters were indeed found to constrain fitness in evolving bacteria (Hughes et al., 2007) and viruses (Alto et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on stochastic environmental effects.

claim: Irregular antibiotic sequences have potential to inhibit bacterial resistance evolution.
source: We show that irregular antibiotic sequences have potential to inhibit bacterial resistance evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Negative hysteresis was identified for multiple combinations of the three β-lactams.
source: Unexpectedly, we further identified negative hysteresis for multiple combinations of the three β-lactams.
evidence: This is a finding from the hysteresis experiments.

claim: Cumulative hysteresis levels per treatment did not significantly associate with any of the measured evolutionary responses.
source: However, cumulative hysteresis levels per treatment did not significantly associate with any of our measured evolutionary responses.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis.

claim: In the previous study with CAR-CIP-GEN, negative hysteresis was expressed for the switches from CAR to GEN and CIP to GEN.
source: In our previous study (Roemhild et al., 2018), within the CAR-CIP-GEN combination, negative hysteresis was expressed for the switches from CAR to GEN and CIP to GEN.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research for comparison.

claim: Only the CAR-GEN hysteresis was significantly associated to the evolutionary responses in the previous study.
source: Yet, only the CAR-GEN hysteresis was significantly associated to the evolutionary responses.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research for comparison.

claim: Hysteresis interactions can exist between antibiotics from the same or different classes, but they need not impact the evolutionary outcome of a sequential treatment protocol each time.
source: Thus, hysteresis interactions can exist between antibiotics from the same or different classes, but they need not impact the evolutionary outcome of a sequential treatment protocol each time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing current and previous results.

claim: In the current study, spontaneous resistance effects and the resulting cross-resistance effects appear to be dominant over the β-lactam hysteresis.
source: In the current study, it appears that spontaneous resistance effects and the resulting cross-resistance effects are dominant over the β-lactam hysteresis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relative importance of different factors.

claim: One potential explanation for the lack of hysteresis impact could be that insensitivity to β-lactam hysteresis evolves quickly.
source: One potential explanation could be that insensitivity to β-lactam hysteresis evolves quickly.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: It warrants further research to assess whether negative hysteresis between the β-lactam drugs is robustly shown across strains of P. aeruginosa or other bacterial species.
source: Nevertheless, it clearly warrants further research to assess whether negative hysteresis between the β-lactam drugs is robustly shown across strains of P. aeruginosa or other bacterial species and can somehow be exploited in sequential therapy, in analogy to the previous results with antibiotics from different classes (Roemhild et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The available antibiotics offer unexplored, highly potent treatment options that can be harnessed to counter the spread of drug resistance.
source: Taken together, our study highlights that the available antibiotics offer unexplored, highly potent treatment options that can be harnessed to counter the spread of drug resistance.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The study underscores the importance of evolutionary trade-offs such as reduced cross-resistance in treatment design.
source: It further underscores the importance of evolutionary trade-offs such as reduced cross-resistance in treatment design
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The study introduces spontaneous resistance rates of component antibiotics as a guiding principle for sequential treatments.
source: and introduces spontaneous resistance rates of component antibiotics as a guiding principle for sequential treatments.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The differential cross-resistance landscape of the β-lactams was a key factor contributing to treatment potency.
source: It is ironic that the differential cross-resistance landscape of the β-lactams was a key factor contributing to treatment potency, even though the risk of cross-resistance is usually used to reject β-lactam-exclusive treatments.
evidence: This is a main conclusion highlighting an ironic finding.

claim: The underlying reasons for differential spontaneous and long-term cross-resistance between these drugs (including the underlying molecular mechanisms) are as yet unknown.
source: The underlying reasons for differential spontaneous and long-term cross-resistance between these drugs (including the underlying molecular mechanisms) are as yet unknown and clearly deserve further attention in the future.
evidence: This acknowledges a knowledge gap.

claim: A detailed understanding of both spontaneous resistance rates and resulting cross-resistances against different antibiotics should be of particular value to further improve the potency of sequential protocols.
source: We conclude that a detailed understanding of both spontaneous resistance rates and resulting cross-resistances against different antibiotics should be of particular value to further improve the potency of sequential protocols.
evidence: This is a final conclusion and recommendation from the study.

claim: All experiments were performed with P. aeruginosa UCBPP-PA14.
source: All experiments were performed with P. aeruginosa UCBPP-PA14 (Rahme et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Bacteria were grown in M9 minimal medium supplemented with glucose (2 g/L), citrate (0.58 g/L), and casamino acids (1 g/L).
source: Bacteria were grown in M9 minimal medium supplemented with glucose (2 g/L), citrate (0.58 g/L), and casamino acids (1 g/L) or on M9 minimal agar (1.5%) or Lysogeny broth (LB) agar.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Cultures and plates were incubated at 37°C.
source: Cultures and plates were incubated at 37°C.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Every treatment consisted of 12 replicate populations (initiated from six biological replicates × two technical replicates).
source: Every treatment consisted of 12 replicate populations (initiated from six biological replicates × two technical replicates).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: All populations were started with an inoculum of 5 × 10^5 cells.
source: All populations were started with an inoculum of 5 × 105 cells.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Populations were propagated as 100 µL batch cultures in 96-well plates, with a transfer to fresh medium every 12 hr (transfer size 2% v/v).
source: Populations were propagated as 100 µL batch cultures in 96-well plates, with a transfer to fresh medium every 12 hr (transfer size 2% v/v).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Growth was monitored by OD600 measurements taken every 15 min through the entire evolution experiment.
source: We monitored growth by OD600 measurements taken every 15 min through the entire evolution experiment (BioTek Instruments, USA; EON; 37°C, 180 rpm double-orbital shaking).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: The evolution experiments were carried out for a total of 96 transfers.
source: The evolution experiments were carried out for a total of 96 transfers.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Populations frozen at transfers 12 and 48 were characterized in detail because they represented the early and late phases of the evolution experiment.
source: We characterized populations frozen at transfers 12 and 48 in detail because they represented the early and late phases of the evolution experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail explaining the rationale for time point selection.

claim: 20 colonies from each population were picked randomly for resistance characterization.
source: After incubation at 37°C, 20 colonies from each population were picked randomly and frozen in 10% (v/v) DMSO and stored at −80°C.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Three isolates per population were chosen for whole-genome sequencing to determine possible targets of selection.
source: From the frozen isolates at transfer 12, we chose three isolates per population (i.e., three biological replicates per population) for whole-genome sequencing to determine possible targets of selection.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: DNA was extracted using a modified CTAB protocol and sequenced using Illumina Nextera DNA Flex library preparation and the MiSeq paired-end technology (2 × 300 bp).
source: We extracted DNA using a modified CTAB protocol (von der Schulenburg et al., 2001) and sequenced it at the Competence Centre for Genomic Analysis Kiel (CCGA Kiel; Institute for Clinical Microbiology, University Hospital Kiel), using Illumina Nextera DNA Flex library preparation and the MiSeq paired-end technology (2 × 300 bp).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: All variants detected in the no drug control were removed as they likely represent adaptation to the medium and not the antibiotic.
source: We removed all variants that were detected in the no drug control as they likely represent adaptation to the medium and not the antibiotic.
evidence: This is a methodological detail explaining data filtering.

claim: The fasta files of all sequenced isolates are available from NCBI under the BioProject number: PRJNA704789.
source: The fasta files of all sequenced isolates are available from NCBI under the BioProject number: PRJNA704789.
evidence: This is a data availability statement.

claim: Hysteresis testing followed the previously developed protocol.
source: The presence of cellular hysteresis was tested, following the previously developed protocol (Roemhild et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation.

claim: Bacterial cells were treated with IC75 of the first antibiotic for 15 min at 37°C and 150 rpm (pretreatment).
source: Bacterial cells were grown to exponential phase (OD600 = 0.08), diluted 10-fold, and treated with IC75 of the first antibiotic. In the treatments where the pretreatment did not require an antibiotic, none was added. These cells were allowed to incubate for 15 min at 37°C and 150 rpm (pretreatment).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: After pretreatment, the first antibiotic was removed by centrifugation and fresh medium containing IC75 of a second antibiotic was added for 8 hr incubation (main treatment).
source: After this, the first antibiotic was removed by centrifugation and fresh medium containing IC75 of a second antibiotic was added. In cases where the main treatment did not require an antibiotic, fresh medium without an antibiotic was added. Bacteria were now incubated for 8 hr at 37°C and 150 rpm (main treatment).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Three biological replicates per treatment and four technical replicates per biological replicate were used for CFU counting in hysteresis experiments.
source: We used three biological replicates per treatment and, for CFU counting, four technical replicates per biological replicate and treatment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: MIC was determined according to the EUCAST protocol modified to account for inoculum effect.
source: We determined the MIC on M9 agar for the antibiotics CAR, CEF, and DOR according to the EUCAST protocol (https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1469-0691.2000.00142.x) that was modified to account for inoculum effect in our fluctuation assay setup.
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation.

claim: 5 × 10^5 cells were spread on M9 agar plates containing doubling dilutions of the antibiotic for MIC determination.
source: 5 × 105 cells were taken from the stationary phase cultures and spread on M9 agar plates containing doubling dilutions of the antibiotic.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Resistance rates were measured using the classic fluctuation assay.
source: We measured resistance rates on the three β-lactams using the classic fluctuation assay (Luria and Delbrück, 1943).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation.

claim: 30 parallel cultures were used for the fluctuation assay, all having a starting concentration of 10^2 CFU/mL.
source: This primary culture was used to start 30 parallel cultures all having a starting concentration of 102 CFU/mL.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: 5 × 10^5 cells were plated onto MIC plates of CAR, CEF, and DOR after 20 hr incubation of parallel cultures.
source: Thereafter, 5 × 105 cells were plated onto MIC plates of CAR, CEF, and DOR.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Resistance rates were estimated using the package rSalvador in R.
source: We used counts from all 30 cultures to estimate resistance rate on each antibiotic using the package rSalvador (Zheng, 2017) in R (R Development Core Team, 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citations.

claim: Sixty mutants with genetic resistance to a given β-lactam were patched onto MIC plates of the two other β-lactams to assess cross-resistance.
source: Sixty mutants with genetic resistance to a given β-lactam were considered biological replicates and patched onto MIC plates of the two other β-lactams.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.
